eligibility.note: A group signature scheme whose core mechanism is an adapted Groth-Ostrovsky-Sahai NIZK proof that hides the signer identity.

qa.evidence: Anonymity and traceability are proven by reduction to the Subgroup Decision and CDH assumptions, in the BMW/BBS security model. Costs are stated only asymptotically as O(k) and as 2k+3 pairings, with no measurements. Related work is compared qualitatively, and the only limitation noted is the cost of verification.

rq2.proof_size: Signature has 2k+3 group elements in G (O(k), logarithmic in the number of signers)
rq2.prover_cost: O(k) signing time
rq2.verifier_cost: O(k); 2k+3 pairings, or 2 multi-pairings plus k exponentiations with batching

rq3.workload: NR
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: NR

rq4.statement_proven: The encrypted (hidden) signer identity bits are well formed (each bit is 0 or 1), and the hidden signature is a valid two-level hierarchical signature on ID.M
rq4.proof_system_used: Adapted Groth-Ostrovsky-Sahai NIZK over composite-order bilinear groups (BGN encryption/commitments)
rq4.reason_for_choice: It gives a standard-model (no random oracle) group signature of logarithmic size, avoiding generic circuit-based NIZK

cq.note: NR

rq5.limitations: Verification needs 2k+3 pairings, which limits practicality. The scheme is built in composite-order groups, and its security rests on the Subgroup Decision assumption.
rq5.open_problems: Move the scheme to prime-order groups, for example under Decision Linear, as the authors suggest. Extend the framework to other extensions such as delegation, revocation and selective revelation.

eligibility.note: Proposes a transparent zk verifiable polynomial delegation scheme and the Virgo succinct zero-knowledge argument for layered circuits.

qa.evidence: Full proofs of Theorems 1-3 are given in the appendices, with simulators in Figures 4-5. Experiments are on an AMD Ryzen 3800X (single core) and a 16-core server, with circuit sizes and baselines (Libra, Hyrax, Ligero, Bulletproofs, Stark, Aurora). The paper says 'We plan to open source our system', and Table II gives an asymptotic comparison.

rq2.proof_size: O(D log C + log^2 n); 253KB for a Merkle tree with 256 leaves (~2^26 gates)
rq2.prover_cost: O(C + n log n); 53.40s for a circuit of 2^26 gates
rq2.verifier_cost: O(D log C + log^2 n) for regular circuits; 50ms for a Merkle tree with 256 leaves

rq3.workload: Matrix multiplication (4x4 to 256x256), image scaling (Lanczos, 112x112 to 1072x1072), Merkle tree with SHA-256 (16 to 256 leaves, up to ~2^26 gates)
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: zkVPD prover 8-10x faster than the pairing-based zkVPD [72]. Virgo prover 7-10x faster than Libra on matrix multiplication and image scaling, and 3-5x faster on the Merkle tree. Verification 10-30x faster than Libra. Prover at least an order of magnitude faster than the other transparent systems.

rq4.statement_proven: Correct evaluation of a layered arithmetic circuit on a secret witness (C(x;w)=1), and correct evaluation of a committed polynomial at a point.
rq4.proof_system_used: Virgo: GKR with a transparent zkVPD built on univariate sumcheck, an RS low-degree test and Merkle trees.
rq4.reason_for_choice: Removes the trusted setup of Libra and the exponentiation and pairing costs, giving fast proving and a lightweight, plausibly post-quantum design.

cq.note: NR

rq5.limitations: The proof size is larger than pairing-based schemes (30-40x for the zkVPD, 253KB vs 90KB for Libra's Merkle tree proof). Succinct verification needs regular circuits.
rq5.open_problems: Reduce proof size using vector commitments with constant-size proofs, and apply the technique to generic ZKP schemes such as Ligero and Aurora for succinct verification.

eligibility.note: vSQL builds a verifiable SQL system on an interactive-proof (CMT/GKR) protocol plus a new extractable polynomial-delegation scheme, so succinct-argument building blocks are the core mechanism.

qa.evidence: Security definition (Def. 3) and assumptions (q-SDH, power knowledge of exponent) are explicit, with a proof of Theorem 3 in Appendix B. The Theorem 4 proof is given only in outline in Appendix C. Evaluation uses TPC-H on EC2 c4.8xlarge with 10 runs per point and compares against IntegriDB and libsnark; no artifact URL is given for vSQL.

rq2.proof_size: Polynomial delegation: O(1) group elements for the commitment; proof of O(ℓ) G elements and O(ℓ·d) F elements. End-to-end communication under half a megabyte in the experiments; 86.4KB for query #15.
rq2.prover_cost: Server runs in O(|C|·log S' + (|B|+|D|)·polylog(|B|+|D|)). Measured: about 0.11ms per input for polynomial delegation and about 1.7µs per gate for CMT. Server time was 2,421s to 5,172s on TPC-H queries #2, #5, #6 and #19.
rq2.verifier_cost: Client runs in O(k + d·polylog(S) + ⌈|B|/|D|⌉·log|D|). Measured 112ms to 427ms on TPC-H queries #2, #5, #6 and #19.

rq3.workload: TPC-H queries #2, #5, #6, #15 and #19 on a database whose largest table has 6×10^6 rows and 13 columns; circuits of up to 945,828,996 gates.
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Server time is 5× (query #6) to 120× (query #5) lower than libsnark-based SNARKs, whose numbers are estimates for hardcoded circuits. Compared with IntegriDB, vSQL is about 23% faster at the server and 36% faster at the client on query #19. Setup is about 295× faster than IntegriDB, whose setup time is estimated.

rq4.statement_proven: The result of an arbitrary SQL query, or the new digest after an update, is correct for the committed outsourced database. The statement is y=C(D,B) for a non-deterministic arithmetic circuit C.
rq4.proof_system_used: CMT/GKR interactive proof with sum-check, plus a new extractable pairing-based multivariate polynomial-delegation scheme.
rq4.reason_for_choice: The information-theoretic protocol limits cryptographic work to the linear input and output size rather than the circuit size, avoids query-specific preprocessing, and supports dynamic updates.

cq.note: The paper footnotes that an earlier version had a flawed polynomial-delegation scheme, which was corrected. It does not study this as a failure class.

rq5.limitations: Optimizations do not cover all SQL queries. Turing-complete SQL variants need general reductions to circuits, and substring and wildcard queries are unsupported. The polynomial-delegation scheme relies on a knowledge-type assumption with benign auxiliary input and needs public parameters that grow with the database size.
rq5.open_problems: Handling substring and wildcard queries, and other operations that arise in natural SQL queries, efficiently.

eligibility.note: SNARK (QAP-based, libsnark) is a core mechanism of a commit-and-prove protocol for verifiable and fair outsourced ML training.

qa.evidence: Threat model: malicious-but-rational server, honest-but-curious client. Soundness is argued informally with a sampling bound (Eq. 4-5); security rests on the underlying VC scheme. Table I reports KeyGen/Prove/Verify times and key sizes; hardware is given, but baselines are only native circuit execution. No code URL is given.

rq2.proof_size: 288 bytes per proof (constant); 256-bit identifier; about 317KB for 10K iterations with 15 proofs
rq2.prover_cost: Linear in circuit size. Per iteration: 0.46-0.51 s (linear regression, batch 32-128), 12.0-16.7 s (NN, batch 32-128). Proving the claimed workload takes about 2.2% of native execution time (linear regression, 100K iterations).
rq2.verifier_cost: 5.9-7.5 ms per iteration (linear regression); 989-1231 ms (NN, batch 32-128). About 10-15 challenged iterations are enough (95%/99% detection).

rq3.workload: Training of linear regression, logistic regression, NN (784-128-128), SVM, K-Means and decision tree on BHP, US, MNIST and Nursery datasets
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Server proving cost is about 2.2% of native execution time (linear regression, 100K iterations, 70% genuine, batch 128, interval 50). Verification is far cheaper than re-execution. Native baseline is the circuit run in jsnark.
rq3.memory: EK size 11.7-189.5 MB and VK size 0.01-70.9 MB (Table I); checkpoint storage 10.2KB for 10K iterations

rq4.statement_proven: A sampled training iteration was correctly executed, mapping the previous state and a data batch to an output state that matches the committed hash identifier. This lets the client verify the training workload without learning the model.
rq4.proof_system_used: libsnark/jsnark QAP-based SNARK (Pinocchio-style), plus a hash-locked ZKCP-style SHA256 blockchain payment contract
rq4.reason_for_choice: SNARK offers succinct proofs, zero-knowledge, and rich expressiveness; proving cost is borne by a powerful server. Arithmetic circuits suit ML multiplications.

cq.note: The paper discusses ZKCP attacks and malicious client-chosen CRS, and mitigates them through protocol design. It does not study bugs as such.

rq5.limitations: Soundness is probabilistic via sampling and relies on the assumption that no shortcut beats the real training algorithm. Delivery correctness of the model is not verified: encryption correctness would need an expensive AES circuit, and the trusted setup is needed.
rq5.open_problems: Malicious aborts and DoS in MLaaS lack a satisfactory deposit-and-refund solution. Better SNARK efficiency and better approximations of non-linear functions are also left open.

Theorems 4 and 1 are proven in the text, but the proofs of Theorems 2, 3, 5 and Lemma 1 are deferred to the full version. The only numeric result is an example parameter set (n=1000, m=40, error 2^-43 + (1/2)^d); there is no empirical evaluation, and the website mention does not give a code URL.

rq2.verifier_cost: NR

rq3.speedup_and_baseline: NR

rq4.statement_proven: Each tallied ballot commitment E = Com(N^i; r) hides an encoded candidate with i in [0, m-1], where N = n+1
rq4.proof_system_used: Custom Sigma protocol over lifted ElGamal commitments, with challenges extracted from voter coin flips and repeated k times (ZK amplification)
rq4.reason_for_choice: E2E verifiability in the standard model, with no CRS or random oracle, against a computationally unbounded EA, using weak voter randomness (min-entropy)

eligibility.note: Zero-knowledge proofs of shuffle, including a new batched variant, are a core mechanism of the GORAM construction.

qa.evidence: Attacker model (honest owner, malicious clients, honest-but-curious server) and security games are explicit; proofs are deferred to a cited ePrint report. Evaluation gives hardware (Xeon 8 cores; EC2 plus MacBook i7), block and DB sizes, client counts, and a Path-ORAM baseline. No code URL is given for GORAM; only a third-party ZK library is cited.

rq2.proof_size: NR
rq2.prover_cost: Computation and communication O((B+G) log N) per operation; batched shuffle proof cost depends on the repetition count k rather than the block size (linear in k).
rq2.verifier_cost: Server verification takes 15-345 ms (S-/A-GORAM, varying block size); batched shuffle soundness is at least 1/2 per iteration, i.e. 1-1/2^k after k repetitions.

rq3.workload: Read/write over a Path-ORAM tree with shuffle proofs; 1GB-1TB storage, 4KB-1MB blocks, 1-10000 clients.
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Batched shuffle proofs greatly outperform off-the-shelf shuffle proofs (no figures stated in text). S-GORAM client read 0.981s vs Path-ORAM 0.042s (1GB, 128KB block, 100 clients). Combined overhead vs Path-ORAM is 7% (read) and 8% (write) for a 1MB block.
rq3.memory: Client storage O(B log N); server storage O(BN).

rq4.statement_proven: The client's uploaded path is a correct permutation and rerandomization of the downloaded path; also knowledge of write permission (predicate-only decryption) and index preservation.
rq4.proof_system_used: Bayer-Groth shuffle argument with a batching step, Groth-Sahai NIZK, plaintext-equivalence proofs, Fiat-Shamir.
rq4.reason_for_choice: Lets the server verify client operations without learning the access pattern; batching removes the dependency on block size.

rq5.limitations: Honest-but-curious server and non-collusion with clients are required for some properties. A-/S-GORAM give up anonymity and rely on an expensive blame procedure and a log. The original GORAM does not scale to large entries and many users.
rq5.open_problems: Relax the server-behavior assumptions and protect access patterns from unauthorized clients. Design solutions letting clients learn only limited information (e.g., statistics) about the dataset.

eligibility.note: Delegated zkSNARK proving (PIOP+KZG) with MPC is the core subject of the paper.

No artifact URL for Siniel; only arkworks cited; limitations only briefly noted (weaker honest-majority security than EOS).

rq2.prover_cost: Delegator: offline share/tag/Beaver-triple generation only; no online interaction. Delegator time at 2^20 and 10MBps: 419 s vs EOS 503 s vs naive Marlin 1549 s
rq2.verifier_cost: NR

rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Delegator at 10MBps: 6.5 s vs EOS 8.8 s (SHA256); at 1000MBps: 0.17 s vs EOS 2.07 s; at 2^20 and 10MBps: 419 s vs naive Marlin 1549 s (~3x) and EOS 503 s (~1.2x)

rq2.prover_cost: Subliminal embedding of b bits costs O(2^(b/2)) point additions plus hash evaluations; proof generation took 3.0087s with the channel vs 2.8412s for a random proof
rq2.verifier_cost: NR

rq3.workload: Zcash Sapling proof generation in the official wallet v2.0.5-2, fully shielded transaction with 1 input and 2 outputs
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: About 6% proof-time overhead (3.0087s vs 2.8412s for a random proof); not an acceleration

rq4.statement_proven: Zcash Sapling spend and output validity (value commitment integrity, spend authority, double-spend prevention) via Groth16
rq4.proof_system_used: Groth16 zk-SNARK (Sapling) and Pedersen commitments
rq4.reason_for_choice: NR

eligibility.note: Collaborative zk-SNARKs (MPC-based distributed proving for Groth16, Marlin, Plonk, Fractal) are the core contribution.

qa.evidence: Definition 1 gives a formal security definition and Theorem 1 gives a proof sketch reducing to the zk-SNARK and MPC security. Evaluation reports GCP n2-standard-2 machines (1 core, 8GB, 3Gb/s), 2^1 to 2^20 constraints, and a single-prover baseline. Code is at github.com/alex-ozdemir/multiprover-snark, and a Discussion section covers limitations (trusted setup, relation leakage, Ω(n) communication).

rq2.proof_size: Constant-size for Groth16/Marlin/Plonk-based collaborative proofs (same as the underlying SNARK). Fractal-based variant grows by a factor of N.
rq2.prover_cost: Groth16, Marlin and Plonk: no more than about 1x (GSZ, honest majority) or about 2x (SPDZ, dishonest majority) single-prover time on 3Gb/s links for large constraint counts (≳2^10). Communication is Θ(λn), with a conditional Ω(n) lower bound.
rq2.verifier_cost: Same as the underlying SNARK (unchanged). Fractal variant grows by a factor of N.

rq3.workload: R1CS instances of 2^1 to 2^20 constraints; Groth16, Marlin and Plonk proofs; 2 or 3 parties (up to 2^5 parties in the party-scaling experiment, Groth16 at 2^10 constraints); an example of about 2900 transactions across 3 banks
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: No speedup. Compared with a single-prover SNARK: 3PC GSZ runs in about the same time (about 1x); SPDZ runs in about 2x the time. For example, 3 banks prove about 2900 transactions (2^20 constraints) in about 165 s.
rq3.memory: Missing data points in Fig. 8 indicate memory exhaustion on 8GB machines; no other memory figures reported.

rq4.statement_proven: A relation over witnesses held by multiple parties, e.g., aggregate healthcare statistics, credit scores, private transaction-graph audits, and net assets above a threshold T, each consistent with Merkle commitments to local data.
rq4.proof_system_used: Groth16, Marlin and Plonk (KZG) run as MPC with SPDZ and GSZ over elliptic-curve secret sharing; Fractal is analysed only.
rq4.reason_for_choice: Their provers consist mostly of linear operations (FFT, MSM, public polynomial division), which are cheap on secret shares. Fractal's Merkle hashing is hard to run in MPC.

cq.note: NR

rq5.limitations: The approach cannot handle programs that branch on shared data or access shared memory locations. It needs a trusted setup, leaks relation membership, and gives only distributed knowledge soundness. Fractal-based collaborative proofs cost N times larger proofs and verification.
rq5.open_problems: Evaluate other MPC protocols with less communication, multi-threading and parallelism, and the effect of latency. Extend to RAM programs by translating them into circuits.

qa.evidence: Formal definitions (Defs 3-9) and Theorems 1-6 are proven under q-PKE, q-PDH and q-SDH. The text gives no hardware or measured numbers (the evaluation sections are absent from this text). The authors say they 'plan to make the code available'.

rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Abstract: up to two orders of magnitude cheaper state sharing than prior QAP approaches; five orders of magnitude better than prior bootstrapped systems. Detailed numbers are not in this text.

rq5.open_problems: NR

eligibility.note: Verifiable SQL scheme with succinct, pairing-accumulator-based proofs relying on an extractability assumption; it has no zero-knowledge property, so eligibility rests on the succinct-argument criterion (IC2).

qa.evidence: The ADS security game is defined formally and assumptions are named (q-SBDH, extractability, CRHF); proofs are only sketched. Asymptotic costs and measured numbers are given on an EC2 machine with 16GB RAM, with libsnark and SNARKs for C as baselines (the latter estimated). A project URL (integridb.github.io) is given and Section 5.2 lists limitations.

rq2.proof_size: Set ops: O(d) proof size for d operations. Range queries: O(d log n). JOIN and nested queries: Õ(|R|). SUM: O(1). Measured: 27.97KB for JOIN on 100,000 rows; 251KB for a 10-dimensional range query; 184.16KB for TPC-H Q19.
rq2.prover_cost: Setup O(sum m_i^2 n_i). Prover time grows linearly in n and d. Measured: about 5000s for a 10-dimensional range query on 100,000 rows; 168s for JOIN on 100,000 rows; 6422.13s for TPC-H Q19. Update O(m^2 log n).
rq2.verifier_cost: Range query O(d log n + |R|). JOIN Õ(|R|). Measured: 45ms for JOIN on 100,000 rows; about 400ms for a 10-dimensional range query; 232ms for TPC-H Q19.

rq3.workload: Verifiable SQL on TPC-H (Q19; tables of 6M and 200K rows) and TPC-C, plus synthetic tables of up to 100,000 rows with up to 10 columns.
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Versus libsnark on a 10-dimensional SUM query (10 columns, 1,000 rows): setup 13.878s vs 157.163s; prover 10.4201s vs 328.830s. Versus SNARKs for C (estimated): prover 10.4201s vs 1000s. Proof size is 84,296B vs 288B and verification 112ms vs 7ms, so IntegriDB is worse on both.
rq3.memory: Server storage is 1.85GB for a table of 10 columns and 100,000 rows, against a 30MB table. Memory limits forced preprocessing of only 4 columns per table for TPC-H.

rq4.statement_proven: The result R of a SQL query (multidimensional range, JOIN, SUM/COUNT/AVG/MAX/MIN, limited nesting) over an outsourced database equals Q(D) relative to a digest.
rq4.proof_system_used: Bilinear-accumulator authenticated set operations (ASO) combined with authenticated interval trees (AIT) built on Merkle trees and skip lists.
rq4.reason_for_choice: Generic verifiable-computation systems (circuit-based and RAM-based) are inefficient for SQL and do not support efficient updates. Prior authenticated data structures lack succinct JOIN, nested-query and multidimensional range support.

cq.note: NR

rq5.limitations: No short proofs for comparisons or aggregations between columns, and JOIN with duplicates inside nested queries is unsupported. Setup is expensive (quadratic in columns), server storage overhead is large, LIKE queries are not supported on dynamic databases, and proofs are larger than those of generic SNARKs.
rq5.open_problems: Removing the no-duplicates assumption for JOIN on range-query results, and supporting LIKE queries in dynamic databases.

eligibility.note: Malicious-secure PSI-sum protocol whose core mechanism is sigma-protocol zero-knowledge proofs (new ZK relations, batching, range proofs with slack, shuffle proofs).

qa.evidence: Ideal/real malicious security model, q-DHI and strong RSA assumptions stated; proofs in appendices A and B. Tables 3, 4 and 6 give communication, computation and cost for input sizes 2^12 to 2^20 against DDH, HEK12 and RR17b baselines. Hardware is only described as Intel Xeon E5 with 3.75 GB; no code URL; limitations appear only as passing remarks.

rq2.proof_size: Batched sigma protocols give sublinear O(sqrt(n)) communication in the proofs; the Bayer-Groth shuffle proof has O(sqrt(n)) communication. Total protocol communication is linear in n: 275,675 KB (low-comm) and 436,719 KB (low-comp) at n=2^20.
rq2.prover_cost: Linear in n for the whole protocol; O(n log n) computation in the sublinear-communication instantiation. Measured at n=2^20: 284,075 s (low-comm) and 35,583 s (low-comp).

rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Communication is 4.21x to 5.03x that of the semi-honest DDH protocol (low-comm). Monetary cost is about 24-25x that of the semi-honest protocol. Versus the HEK12 Sort-Compare-Shuffle malicious baseline, communication is about 250x lower and monetary cost about 64x lower at 2^20 (low-comp variant).

rq4.statement_proven: Correct DOPRF evaluation under committed keys, correct shuffle/re-randomization, correct CS and ElGamal encryption and commitment consistency, range bounds with slack, and correct partial decryption.
rq4.proof_system_used: Fiat-Shamir sigma protocols with batching, Bayer-Groth shuffle and multi-exponentiation arguments, Pedersen commitments, Camenisch-Shoup and ElGamal encryption.
rq4.reason_for_choice: Sigma protocols allow efficient proofs about committed and encrypted values without trusted setup, and batching reduces communication, which is the dominant cost in practice.

cq.note: Verifiable generation of Pedersen, CS and ElGamal parameters removes the need for a trusted setup.

rq5.limitations: The final intersection-sum must lie in a polynomial domain because exponential ElGamal needs a discrete log for decryption. Computation is far higher than the semi-honest and Sort-Compare-Shuffle protocols, and the PRF has only selective security for exponential domains.

eligibility.note: PEREA is an anonymous authentication scheme whose core mechanism is a set of ZKPoK protocols, with a new construction and a security proof.

qa.evidence: Security goals are defined formally in Appendix A, and the proof is only sketched (Appendix B) and reduces to Strong RSA and DDH. rq2.proof_size: Uplink communication O(K), where K is the revocation window size; downlink O(L) for the blacklist, with 166-bit entries.
rq2.prover_cost: User computation O(L) + O(K∆L). Measured worst case for the user is 5.9s at K=10, L=800; it is 0.7s when ∆L=100 and K=10.

rq3.workload: Anonymous authentication with blacklist sizes L up to 800 and revocation windows K=5, 10, 15 and 30.
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Server time is constant, at 0.05s (K=5) and 0.16s (K=30), versus 2.9s for BLAC at L=800. User time is slower than BLAC.

rq4.statement_proven: The user holds a signed queue of the K most recent tickets, none of which is in the blacklist accumulator. The current ticket is well formed and the commitment to the next queue is correct.
rq4.proof_system_used: Sigma-style ZKPoK built from the Camenisch-Lysyanskaya block signature, Li et al. universal accumulator non-membership proofs and RSA-group commitments.
rq4.reason_for_choice: Allows revocation without a TTP, with server cost that does not depend on blacklist size.

cq.note: The paper describes a timing attack and a concurrency issue as discussion points. It does not study or detect failure classes of ZKP implementations.

rq5.limitations: The user computation is higher than in BLAC, and the revocation window K limits how fast users can authenticate. The ZKPoK is not secure under concurrent execution, so authentication runs sequentially.
rq5.open_problems: Removing the critical section that forces sequential authentication.
